newsitem.title: USA: CBOT panel says weather to override USDA crop data.
newsitem.headline: CBOT panel says weather to override USDA crop data.

text.p: Weather patterns this summer will overshadow Monday's government crop production and supply/demand reports, said analysts on a panel assembled by the Chicago Board of Trade.

"Overall there were no dramatic surprises that should move the futures one way or another," said Jack Scoville, vice president of Price Futures Group, Chicago of expected trade reactions over the next several months to USDA data.
The U.S. Agriculture Department on Monday released its May crop output and supply/demand reports.
However, analysts agreed that the reports still had the capability of influencing futures trade on a short-term basis.
However, analysts agreed that the government reports may well influence futures markets on a short-term basis.
Analysts called CBOT soybean futures to open three to five cents per bushel lower while corn and wheat were called to open one to two cents lower after this morning's reports.

The government said 1997 U.S. soybean production would be a record 2.6 billion bushels, corn would be the second highest on record at 9.84 billion and winter wheat production would total 1.561 billion bushels.
"As long as the weather stays good over the next few months we do have a chance to attain those levels," Scoville said.
Steve Bruce, grain broker and floor manager for E.D. and F. Man International agreed that weather will dominate the markets and cited mounting concern about Kansas wheat belt conditions.
"From this point on we're going to be trading weather and the weather is a little dry in western Kansas," Bruce said.

USDA said 1997 U.S. hard red winter wheat production, the class of wheat grown in Kansas, would total 893.927 million bushels, about in line with an average of analysts' estimates for 894.3 million bushels.
Panelists also noted the USDA had taken into account the freeze damage that occured the weekend of April 12-13 because the government data was based on conditions existing as of May 1.

CBOT soybean futures Monday were called to open three to five cents per bushel lower because USDA did not trim five to 10 million bushels from its 1996-97 U.S. carryout for soybeans as many market watchers expected.
USDA left unchanged its estimate for '96-'97 soybean ending stocks at 125 million bushels.
"There has been some thinking 125 million carryover estimate for soy is a little negative, but that's still a tight carryout," Bruce said.
Corn carryout for 1996-97 was pegged at 909 million bushels versus trade estimates of 869 million to 929 million.
The 1996-97 wheat carryout was pegged by USDA at 465 million bushels, above expectations for 450 million.

USDA lowered the Brazilian 1997 soybean production to 26.5 million tonnes from the previous 27.0 million and dropped its outlook for Argentine soy production to 12.4 million tonnes from the previous 13.25 million.
The CBOT panel said there would be even further cuts in South American soybean production estimates.
"I think there's room for another drop in the numbers for Brazil and Argentina beans," Scoville said.
